You are reviewing a code diff for ALTITUDE issues only: is each change implemented at the right depth, or is it a fragile bandaid / special case layered on shared infrastructure instead of a deeper fix to the underlying mechanism? Do not look for correctness bugs.

Context: this diff is from a session that got a real llama-completion binary running under an "andesim" hybrid RISC-V simulator (QEMU + a cycle-accurate RTL simulator called vsim). The target hardware only supports 32-bit vector elements (ELEN=32) and a narrower float-vector width (LMUL up to 4, not the spec default of 8) than llama.cpp's ggml library assumed. Several ggml functions were crashing with illegal-instruction traps because they emitted vector instructions this hardware can't execute.

Two repos are involved:
1. `/home/nick/work/andesim` (the simulator driver, C++) — diff at `/tmp/claude-1002/-home-nick-work-andesim/5eeca9dc-9078-4a2c-9aec-f331d1142619/scratchpad/simplify_andesim.diff`
2. `/home/nick/work/llama.cpp` (the LLM inference engine, ggml's CPU backend, C) — diff at `/tmp/claude-1002/-home-nick-work-andesim/5eeca9dc-9078-4a2c-9aec-f331d1142619/scratchpad/simplify_llamacpp.diff`

Read both diff files. Note: each diff is the FULL uncommitted diff of the touched files (nothing has been committed this session), so it may include some pre-existing uncommitted work from earlier in the same effort mixed in with the new work — focus your attention on what looks like genuinely NEW logic (added functions, added CLI flags, added helpers), not on isolated pre-existing lines that happen to be nearby.

Four fixes were applied to llama.cpp's ggml, each a DIFFERENT mechanism for what looks like a similar underlying problem (this hardware's vector-unit limits vs. what the code assumes):
1. `ggml_vec_dot_f16`/`ggml_vec_dot_bf16` in `vec.cpp`: fixed with a per-FUNCTION `__attribute__((target("arch=rv64gc")))` (a compiler-flag-level annotation on two specific functions).
2. `ggml_vec_cvar_f32`/`ggml_vec_soft_max_f32` in `vec.cpp`: fixed by rewriting the algorithm itself (removing an unnecessary 64-bit-element widening reduce, replacing with a narrower reduce + scalar widen).
3. `quantize_row_q8_0`/`quantize_row_q8_1` in `arch/riscv/quants.c`: fixed by deleting the vectorized implementation entirely and calling the portable scalar reference implementation instead.
4. (Already existed, elsewhere in the same CMakeLists.txt, not part of this diff but relevant context) a FILE-LEVEL `set_source_files_properties` march override for other generic dispatch files.

Read `/home/nick/work/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/CMakeLists.txt` around line 715-770 for the full picture of how these four mechanisms coexist (function-attribute, algorithm-rewrite, delete-and-fallback, file-level march). Judge: is having FOUR different mechanisms for variants of the same root problem (this target's vector-capability mismatch) a sign of accumulating special cases that should be unified into one deeper mechanism — e.g. a single documented policy or a build-time capability macro that each site checks — or is each one genuinely the right tool for ITS specific shape of problem (auto-vectorized scalar code vs. deliberate-but-wrong-precision intrinsics vs. no-narrower-alternative-exists)? The diff's own comments (read them) argue each is deliberately different because the underlying causes differ. Decide if you buy that reasoning or if there's a deeper unifying fix being missed.

Also check: `driver/cmd_run.cpp`'s new `--step-timeout-ms` handling — is bolting a manual parse-and-validate block directly into `cmd_run.cpp`'s run_hybrid() function the right altitude, or should this level of CLI-value validation live in `cli.cpp`'s parser itself (where `--mem-size` conceptually lives, even though its actual numeric parsing also happens at point-of-use in cmd_run.cpp — check that precedent)?

Report only real findings with file, line, a one-line summary, and what the deeper fix would look like. If you conclude the existing design is already at the right altitude, say so plainly and explain why in 2-3 sentences — do not manufacture a finding to have something to report. Keep the report under 400 words.

Compiles via iree_tuner.py, benchmarks on FPGA, iterates. Use whenever the user mentions tuning IREE dispatch tile sizes, agentic tile search, or wants to replace GA-based tile-size search with LLM-driven search. optimization config, parse FPGA hardware features, extract shapes from perf test files,

## Findings

**1. llama.cpp CMakeLists.txt "four mechanisms" — mostly right altitude, one outlier**

Mechanisms 1 (function `target` attribute), 2 (algorithm rewrite), and 4 (file-level march) hold up under their own stated reasoning: 4 blanket-restricts files with no genuine vector code (cheap, correct); 1 scopes to a scalar *fallback* branch inside an otherwise-legitimate vector file, which file-level policy can't reach; 2 replaces a hand-written intrinsic that hard-assumed e64 with a strictly-better narrower algorithm that's correct on *every* target, not just this one — no capability macro needed because there's no capability trade-off left. These three are genuinely different tools for genuinely different problem shapes, not accumulating cruft.

Mechanism 3 (`ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c:32-54`, `quantize_row_q8_0`/`quantize_row_q8_1`) is the real outlier. It doesn't gate the fix to the narrow-LMUL target — it deletes the `#if defined(__riscv_v)` capability check entirely, so the scalar fallback now runs unconditionally on *every* riscv64+GGML_RVV build, including a hypothetical/future full-spec LMUL=8 chip that has no problem here. Confirmed by checking `CMakeLists.txt:438-513`: this file compiles once per configured variant with no per-function capability dispatch, so there's no other mechanism recovering vectorization for capable hardware. The file's own surrounding convention (sibling functions at `quants.c:158,213,264,318,387,418,499` all still guard with `#if defined(__riscv_v)`) shows this pair is the one place that pattern was abandoned rather than followed. The comment even concedes a narrower fix was available ("QK8_0 is already an exact fit at LMUL=2... isn't worth re-deriving") — that's mechanism 2's approach, not applied here. Deeper fix: either rewrite at LMUL=2 like mechanism 2 did, or gate the scalar-only fallback behind the same capability signal mechanism 4 already established, instead of an ungated global deletion.

**2. andesim `--step-timeout-ms` — right file, duplicated mechanism**

Placement in `cmd_run.cpp`'s `run_hybrid()` (`cmd_run.cpp:612-624`) is correct altitude, not a bandaid: andesim's convention is uniform — `cli.cpp` never validates values (only structural: missing-value/unknown-flag), every flag validates at point-of-use, confirmed by `--mem-size` itself (raw string in `cli.cpp:109`, real parsing via `parse_size`/`qemu_m_args` in `shm.cpp` from `cmd_run.cpp`). Putting validation in `cli.cpp` would break that convention, not follow it.

The real finding: the validation logic is a near-verbatim duplicate of `parse_knob` (`cmd_profile.cpp:214-226`) — same `std::stoi`+full-consumption+`>0` contract — reimplemented inline instead of reused. It can't even be reused as-is: `parse_knob` sits in an anonymous namespace, internal linkage only. Unlike `--mem-size`, which got a named, header-declared, unit-tested helper (`parse_size`, tested in `infra_test.cpp`), this new block is untested in isolation (`cli_test.cpp:247-259` only covers raw-string capture) and unreusable. Deeper fix: hoist one shared `parse_positive_int` helper (e.g., beside `parse_size` in `shm.hpp`) that both `cmd_profile.cpp` and `cmd_run.cpp` call.
